As of 229 PM EST Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain is expected across portions of the area today, 
although amounts will generally be light.

Latest surface analysis depicted two weak surface lows offshore
(one off the coast of VA and the other off the Carolina
coastline). Rain has remained mainly confined to the Piedmont
this afternoon. However, CAMs show the showers pushing NE across
the rest of the area later this afternoon into this evening.
As such, have adjusted PoPs to show the later time of arrival
for the showers across eastern portions of the area. However,
QPF still looks light with generally around 0.25" of rain or 
less across the area (highest totals across the SW). Otherwise,
temps were in the lower 60s across the Piedmont and around 70F
near/along the coast as of 1 PM. Highs this afternoon are
expected to warm into the lower 70s east of I-95 with mid 60s
across the Piedmont. However, it is possible the Piedmont
remains in the lower 60s given N winds and ongoing light rain.
Clouds linger through most of the night with some partial
clearing possible across the NW half of the area. As such, it
will be a mild night with lows in the lower 50s NW to upper 50s
SE.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Mild temperatures are expected Monday followed by cooler 
weather Tuesday.

Low pressure continues to quickly move northeast and away from the 
Mid Atlantic coast Monday. Meanwhile, a cold front will cross
the area during the day. The latest model guidance shows
scattered showers developing along and behind the front Mon 
afternoon into Mon night. The HRRR and RRFS are the most
aggressive with this solution. However, given dew points still 
in the 50s and mild temperatures in the lower 70s for highs, 
just enough instability may be present to support this solution.
As such, have added low-end PoPs across the area for the FROPA.


Cooler air arrives Tuesday as that high builds southward from 
eastern Canada. Dry weather is expected throughout the day, but 
clouds may gradually thicken, especially by Tuesday night. Highs
on Tuesday will only stay in the 50s area-wide, with lows 
dropping back into the mid- upper 20s NW to lower 30s SE inland
and lower 40s along the coast Tuesday night into Wednesday
morning.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Confidence is increasing in an impactful low
pressure system bringing heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal 
flooding Wednesday into Thanksgiving Day.

Attention turns to a more significant low pressure system 
developing during the middle of the week. While uncertainty 
remains regarding the exact track, strength, and timing of the 
system, the latest 12z GFS and ECMWF (and respective ensembles) 
continue to depict low pressure developing off the Southeast 
coast Wednesday before strengthening and tracking northward 
along the Mid Atlantic coast Wednesday night into Thanksgiving 
Day. The most recent trend has been for a more inland storm 
track with many ensemble members now taking the low across 
interior portions of the CWA. This shift inland is due in large 
part to the closed upper level low remaining well to the west 
across the Midwest. That positions of the closed upper level low
leaves a continued inland trend well within the range of 
possibilities. The interaction of the northern stream cutoff low
and the southern stream shortwave acts to further complicate 
the scenario. As such, would not be surprised if it takes a 
while for models to lock in on the track of this system. 
However, while the surface low track remains uncertain, 
confidence remains high in the position and strength of a strong
area of high pressure to the north of the area (1040+ mb). This
will create a strong pressure gradient and baroclinic zone
across the local area regardless of a more inland or offshore
track of the low. NBM wind probs for 40+ mph gusts were 40-70% 
across most inland areas and 70-90% along the coast. Meanwhile, 
EPS probs for 1"+ and 2"+ of rain were 80-90% and 30-60% 
respectively across the area while the GEFS probs were 70-90% 
and 40-60% respectively. As such, a period of strong winds and
widespread rain (potentially heavy) is increasingly likely.

Of potentially greater concern is the combination of strong and
prolonged onshore flow with an approaching period of elevated 
astronomical tides and full moon. Depending on the eventual 
track of the low, increasing tidal departures could result in 
significant coastal flooding along portions of the Chesapeake 
Bay, tidal rivers, and Atlantic coast. Hazardous marine 
conditions also appears increasingly likely (see marine section 
below). 

Given the Thanksgiving holiday and associated travel, this system 
will need to be closely monitored over the coming days. While 
confidence is increasing in the potential for a coastal storm, 
specific rainfall amounts, wind speeds, and coastal flooding impacts 
remain uncertain and will depend heavily on the eventual track and 
intensity of the low. Continue to monitor the forecast over the 
coming days.

KEY M
